scenes.headline: Testing & Mocking
scenes.subtitle: Isolating code from the outside world
scenes.narration: Testing proves your logic is correct, and mocking lets you test that logic in isolation from slow or unreliable external systems like APIs, databases, and the clock.

scenes.headline: Why mock at all
items: Real network and database calls make tests slow and flaky
Some conditions like failures or specific dates are hard to reproduce
You want to test your code, not the third-party service
scenes.narration: Hitting a live API or database in a test makes it slow and dependent on things outside your control, so a passing test today can fail tomorrow for reasons unrelated to your code. Mocking also lets you simulate scenarios that are otherwise painful to trigger, such as a timeout or a specific timestamp. Above all, mocking keeps the spotlight on your own logic rather than on someone else's service.

scenes.headline: Mock vs Stub vs Fake
scenes.narration: A mock is a spy that records the calls made to it, so afterward you can assert that a function was invoked with the right arguments the right number of times. A stub or fake, by contrast, simply returns pre-arranged data to satisfy your code without recording anything. Use a mock when the interaction itself is what you want to verify, and a stub when you only need believable data flowing through.

scenes.headline: Patching an external call
scenes.narration: The patch decorator temporarily replaces requests.get inside myapp with a mock for the duration of the test. We tell that mock to return a fake JSON payload, so the function under test never touches the network. Finally, assert_called_once confirms the code actually made exactly one request, verifying both the result and the behavior.

scenes.headline: Mocking time and randomness
scenes.narration: Non-deterministic inputs like the current time are a frequent source of flaky tests. By patching the datetime used inside the module, we freeze utcnow to a fixed value, making the output of partition_path completely predictable. This same technique of patching a dependency at the point where it is used applies to random numbers, UUIDs, and any other source of variability.

scenes.headline: Testing best practices
items: Patch where an object is used, not where it is defined
Keep tests fast, isolated, and independent of run order
Cover the happy path plus edge cases and error handling
scenes.narration: The single most common mocking mistake is patching the original location of an object rather than the module that imported it, so always patch where it is used. Good tests run quickly and independently, never relying on the order in which they execute. And thorough coverage means going beyond the happy path to include empty inputs, malformed data, and the error branches.

scenes.text: Mock the boundaries of your system so you test your own logic in isolation — fast, deterministic, and reliable.
scenes.narration: Draw a clear line at the edges of your system and mock across it, so every test exercises your own logic in a fast, deterministic way. That discipline is what makes a test suite worth trusting.
